backups.name: Southwest Ridge via High Divide and the Catwalk
backups.grade: Class 2–3 with steep snow early season
gear: bear canister (required in Sol Duc/Seven Lakes Basin)
map & compass or GPS (route beyond High Divide is unsigned)
hazards: The Catwalk — an exposed, sharp ridge crest between Cat Peak and Carrie; a fall here could be fatal
Thin, crumbly ledges with major exposure on Cat Peak's south side just before the Catwalk
Steep, loose, unstable scree on Carrie's south-facing summit basin
No water between Heart Lake and the summit
Unmaintained, unsigned route beyond High Divide requiring solid off-trail Olympics route-finding
backups.overview: Mount Carrie is the highest point of the Bailey Range and the scenic centerpiece of the classic Bailey Range Traverse. There is no trail or known route connecting Hurricane Ridge to Cat Basin or Mount Carrie — Hurricane Ridge sits on the opposite (east) side of the park and is used only as a distant viewpoint of Carrie's glaciated north face. Every recorded ascent instead approaches from the Sol Duc River Road trailhead on the park's north side, via Heart Lake, High Divide, Cat Basin, the exposed "Catwalk" ridge crossing, and Boston Charlie's Camp, before gaining Carrie's southwest ridge and a broad south-facing scree basin to the summit.
backups.beta: This route gains the High Divide crest from Heart Lake, then heads east along the Cat Basin trail toward Cat Peak before crossing the Catwalk—an infamous, exposed ridge-top connecting Cat Peak to Mount Carrie. The Catwalk features high Class 2 to low Class 3 scrambling with substantial exposure; a fall here can be fatal. Beyond the Catwalk, the route follows the southwest ridge of Mount Carrie, initially grassy but becoming a mixture of grass and rock outcroppings at higher elevations, traversing scree and possible snow to the true summit at the far right of the summit basin.
backups.turnaround: On snow, top out before midday softening; the long return to camp makes an early turnaround wise.
backups.face: Long Ridge / Bailey Range crest approach
backups.permit: Olympic National Park: no permit for day climbs; all overnight wilderness stays require a wilderness camping permit via Recreation.gov.
backups.comms: Cell phone coverage is unreliable throughout Olympic National Park. Satellite communicator (Garmin InReach or similar) is strongly recommended.
backups.descent: Reverse the southwest ridge and south-facing scree basin down to Boston Charlie's Camp, re-cross the exposed Catwalk to Cat Peak, then follow High Divide back to Heart Lake and out the Sol Duc River Trail to the trailhead.
obj_haz: exposed unroped scrambling on the Catwalk

waypoints.name: Sol Duc Trailhead
waypoints.directions: Do not drive to Hurricane Ridge — there is no established approach to Carrie from there, and essentially every party starts at Sol Duc instead. From US-101 near Lake Crescent, turn up Sol Duc Hot Springs Road and follow it to the end at the Sol Duc River trailhead, around 2,000 ft. The maintained trail toward Sol Duc Falls and the Deer Lake junction leaves from here.

backups.detailed_rack: A lightweight alpine rack for scrambling: ice axe, crampons, helmet, rope (30–50m rope optional for group safety on Catwalk), and self-rescue equipment. Harness and sling recommended if roping. For water-crossing sections, consider trekking poles for stream fords.
what_to_bring: Layers (high-altitude, wet Pacific weather is common)
High-calorie food and electrolyte drink mix
First aid kit with blister treatment
pro_tips: Start early from Boston Charlie's Camp to ensure you cross the Catwalk in daylight and have time to retreat if weather deteriorates.
Scout the Catwalk carefully in marginal light; the exposure is real and requires full attention.
The loose rock (choss) is typical of the Olympics—expect to pick your way carefully and wear a helmet.
Descending is often more hazardous than ascending on scrambles; move methodically on the way down.
Cache water bottles at Boston Charlie's to avoid carrying excessive weight; melt snow or find streams at higher elevations.
Wildlife is active at dawn and dusk; make noise while traveling.
watch_out: The Catwalk is the crux of the climb—treat it with respect and expect high exposure.
Helmet is mandatory; rockfall is frequent from loose, unstable rock.
Before mid-July, expect deep snow on the Catwalk; ice axe and crampons required.
Wildlife encounter risk; black bears present in the area.
Cell phone coverage is unreliable; carry satellite communication device for emergencies.
backups.pro_needs: Grade Class 2–3 scrambling protection: helmet mandatory for rockfall hazard, ice axe essential for early-season snow and self-arrest, crampons for frozen surfaces June–July. Rope carries psychological security on the Catwalk but is not strictly required for individuals with solid scrambling skills and comfort with exposure; recommended for groups.
backups.best_season: Late July through mid-September for the most reliable dry scree and a snow-free Catwalk crossing; an ice axe is still worth carrying for lingering snow patches into July.
backups.approach: There is no established route to Mount Carrie from Hurricane Ridge; that area is separated from the Bailey Range by miles of trailless, glaciated terrain and functions only as a viewpoint. The actual approach used by essentially all climbers starts at the Sol Duc River Road trailhead (~2,000 ft) on US-101 near Lake Crescent: Sol Duc Falls → Deer Lake Trail junction (+1 mi) → Heart Lake (+7 mi, 4,800 ft) → High Divide crest (+0.5 mi, 5,100 ft) → east on the Cat Basin trail toward Cat Basin → an unmaintained path over Cat Peak's exposed south side and across the airy "Catwalk" ridge (Class 3) to Boston Charlie's Camp. From camp, the final push follows Carrie's southwest ridge (Class 1 grass/rock) and contours a broad, steep, loose south-facing scree basin around 6,500 ft before a scree-and-snow finish (ice axe advisable) to the summit (Class 2). One-way distance from the trailhead to the summit is roughly 13 miles.
backups.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line. From the summit, descend the southwest ridge and the south-facing scree basin below it to Boston Charlie's Camp, keeping the helmet on - the rock here is loose and rockfall is the reason the helmet is mandatory on this route - and carrying the axe for any steep snow still lying in the basin early in the season. From Boston Charlie's, re-cross the Catwalk to Cat Peak. This is the crux of the day in descent exactly as it is in ascent: a narrow rock and heather ridge with substantial exposure where a fall could be fatal, and descending a scramble is generally the more hazardous direction, so cross it in daylight and with full attention rather than hurrying it at the end of a long day. From Cat Peak follow the High Divide back to Heart Lake, then take the Sol Duc River Trail out to the trailhead. There is no rappelling anywhere on the standard line.
backups.bail: Retreat into Cat Basin is feasible; the main commitment is the distance back to the road.

pitch_detail.notes: From the Sol Duc road-end trailhead (~2,000 ft) pass Sol Duc Falls and the Deer Lake junction (about 1 mile) and climb about 7 more miles up the Sol Duc valley to Heart Lake (4,800 ft). The lake has several good camps; a wilderness permit and bear canister are required, and permits here are in heavy demand.
pitch_detail.pitch: Sol Duc TH to Heart Lake

pitch_detail.notes: Climb about half a mile to the High Divide crest (~5,100 ft) and follow it toward Cat Basin, about 3 miles, to where the maintained trail ends. A thin, worn path continues along the ridge below Cat Peak through trees and brush to the start of the Catwalk. Late in the season water up here is limited to snowbanks and sinkholes, so carry enough.

A narrow rock and heather ridgetop links Cat Peak to the Bailey Range: high class 2 to low class 3 moves with serious exposure, where a fall could be fatal. Before mid-July lingering snow can make it much harder. Past it, push through brush to Boston Charlie's Camp, a small, sloping, exposed site with a brackish sinkhole pond; filter the water, and treat it as an emergency bivy rather than a planned camp.

A semi-cairned path switchbacks up Carrie's southwest ridge, about 2,000 ft in under a mile; grassy at first, then grass and rock outcrops as it narrows. Near 6,500 ft it contours around the top of a big south-facing scree basin ringed with summits; the rock is loose, so helmets on. The true summit is at the far right (east) side of the basin, reached via the summit ridge. Early season, snow in the basin calls for an axe.

itinerary.cal: Best mid-July through mid-September once snow clears enough for safe passage across the exposed Catwalk; earlier in the season an ice axe is needed in the summit scree basin.

days.note: Hike the Sol Duc trail past the Deer Lake junction to Heart Lake, the standard base camp for the Cat Basin/Catwalk approach to Carrie.
days.title: Approach to Heart Lake camp

days.note: A genuinely long day: gain the High Divide, drop into Cat Basin, cross the exposed class 3 Catwalk past Boston Charlie's Camp, then climb Carrie's grassy/scree southwest ridge to the summit scree basin and the true summit, before reversing the entire route back to camp.

itinerary.totalNote: A demanding 3-day, roughly 27-mile round trip: two travel days to and from a Heart Lake base camp bookend one very long summit day (the published time is 5 hr from camp; real parties report 9.5-12+ hr) across Cat Basin and the exposed Catwalk to Carrie's summit.

access.fees: $8/person/night camping fee + $6 reservation fee; park entrance $30/vehicle (7-day) or $15/person on foot.
access.notes: No separate climbing cost-recovery fee like Mount Rainier’s $82 — only the standard entrance fee and wilderness camping permit apply.
access.rules: Bear canisters required for food storage in the Sol Duc/Seven Lakes Basin zone (free rental at Port Angeles/Quinault Wilderness Information Centers); groups of 7+ must use designated group sites.
access.permit: NPS Wilderness Permit required for overnight camping, reserved via Recreation.gov within the May 15–Oct 15 quota season (permits release April 15).
access.landManager: Olympic National Park (Daniel J. Evans Wilderness)
access.land_manager: National Park Service — Olympic National Park (Olympic Wilderness)
access.parking_pass: Olympic NP entrance fee: $30/vehicle (7-day), $55 annual Olympic NP pass, or $80 America the Beautiful interagency annual pass.

overnight_permit.what: Olympic National Park wilderness permit, per person per night; Sol Duc and Seven Lakes Basin is a quota area
overnight_permit.where: Reserve on Recreation.gov, or get one in person at a park Wilderness Information Center such as Port Angeles.

road.name: Sol Duc Hot Springs Road (Sol Duc River Road)
road.driveNote: From US-101 near Lake Crescent, drive ~14 miles up Sol Duc Hot Springs Road, past the resort, to the road-end trailhead.
road.seasonalGate: Typically gated/closed by snow late October–late March

climate.typical: Marine west coast climate with heavy orographic precipitation off the Pacific; snow can persist on the Catwalk and summit scree into July even in an average year.

bySeason.fall: Increasingly wet with early-season snow possible after late September.
bySeason.spring: Deep lingering snowpack on High Divide/Catwalk into early summer.
bySeason.summer: Jul–Sep is the reliable window; expect mostly dry weather with occasional frontal passages and cold nights at high camps.
bySeason.winter: Sol Duc Road closed by snow; not a standard-season objective.

emergency.notes: Remote, largely trailless terrain with poor-to-no cell coverage; a serious accident near the Catwalk or Cat Basin will likely require an NPS/county SAR helicopter response.
emergency.rangerStation: Olympic National Park Wilderness Information Center, Port Angeles — 360-565-3100
emergency.nearestHospital: Olympic Medical Center, Port Angeles (939 Caroline St)

crowds.peakTraffic: Late July–August weekends, mostly tied to multi-day Bailey Range Traverse through-trips rather than dedicated Carrie ascents
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Low — likely a few dozen parties per season at most. The whole Bailey Range Traverse (which this route accesses) saw only ~150 wilderness permits issued in 2018; this SE/Cat Basin approach is a subset of that traffic, and standalone ascents of Carrie via this line specifically are uncommon.

fitnessSpec.hiking: Very high — multi-day sustained off-trail travel with major elevation gain/loss; Bailey Range terrain is notoriously strenuous
fitnessSpec.packWeight: 35-45+ lbs for a multi-day trip (overnight camping gear, bear canister, snow gear)

partner_requirements.approachTime: Long — typically one full day on trail to a camp at Heart Lake or Cat Basin, followed by a very long summit day across the Catwalk
requiredSkills: Off-trail route-finding/navigation in trailless alpine terrain
Steep snow travel and self-arrest with an ice axe
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Experienced off-trail scrambler/backpacker comfortable with sustained trailless alpine travel and steep snow; not a beginner scramble given the remoteness and route-finding demands

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July through August, once the early-season snow finger has melted down

July.reason: Steep snow finger often still present on the upper route early in the month, requiring ice axe/self-arrest skill; conditions improve steadily through July

August.reason: Best conditions — snow mostly reduced to isolated patches, tundra terrain open, most stable weather window

September.reason: Still climbable with fewer parties, but shorter days and rising chance of early-season storms/new snow later in the month

weather.typical: Central/north Olympics maritime climate — wetter than the eastern Washington peaks, with a large winter snowpack feeding the Bailey Range snowfields that lingers into early summer
weather.probability: Weather can shift quickly in this interior range; summer is the best window with the snow finger receding through the season

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Off-trail Class 2-3 terrain with steep snow sections early season; fall potential on snow slopes without ice axe/self-arrest ability; very remote location far from any rescue infrastructure

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer route; NWAC does not issue Olympics-zone avalanche forecasts during the July-September climbing season (forecast season runs roughly Nov-Apr)

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: N/A - no glacier travel on this route (steep snowfields, not a glacier)

gaps: Route name references 'Hurricane Ridge,' but no trail or documented approach connects Hurricane Ridge to Cat Basin/Mount Carrie — approach and access fields corrected to the actual Sol Duc trailhead approach; recommend renaming this route to avoid confusing climbers into thinking Hurricane Ridge is a viable start point.
The ~13-mile one-way approach figure is a composite of several trip reports and not an official NPS measurement.

Difficulty breakdown (physical/technical/exposure/commitment/routefinding) is a computed starting estimate derived from grade, pitch count, and route data on file -- not a researched or crowd-sourced rating. Users can blend in their own read via the UI.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Sol Duc Trailhead at the end of Sol Duc Hot Springs Road

backups.rope_note: Route crosses the exposed 'Catwalk' ridge (3rd-class moves with good holds) between Cat Basin and Carrie, described as unmaintained and requiring good route-finding. Early-season snow requires ice axe and crampons; the route is not normally roped.
backups.corrections: None; matches guidebook/trip-report description of the SE Route via Cat Basin/Catwalk.
rack: 30-50m rope (optional, group safety on the exposed Catwalk)
Harness and sling if roping up

approach_variants.name: Sol Duc road end, High Divide and Cat Basin to the Catwalk
approach_variants.notes: Start at the road-end trailhead on the hot-springs road on the park's north side. Hike past the falls, on past the Deer Lake junction, and up to Heart Lake — the last reliable water. Climb to the High Divide crest and follow the primitive trail east from the junction above the lake toward Cat Basin, then take the unmaintained path over the exposed south side of the peak beyond it and across the CATWALK to the first camp on its far side. Do NOT plan an approach from Hurricane Ridge: it is a viewpoint separated from this range by miles of trailless glaciated terrain and there is no established route to this peak from it.
approach_variants.season: Late July to September, once the high traverse is clear of snow; an ice axe is still worth carrying for the summit basin.
hazards: The Catwalk — exposed, sharp, and a fall there could be fatal
Thin, crumbly ledges with major exposure on the south side of the peak just before the Catwalk
Steep, loose, unstable scree in the summit basin
Early-season snow in the basin, where an ice axe is advisable
No water between Heart Lake and the summit
Unmaintained and unsigned beyond the divide, requiring solid off-trail route-finding
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the basin camp, the line follows the peak's SOUTHWEST RIDGE — grassy and rocky walking at first — and the base of the real climbing is where that ridge stops being walkable crest and you have to CONTOUR OFF IT into a broad, steep, loose SOUTH-FACING SCREE BASIN at around sixty-five hundred feet. The test that you are in the right basin: it is loose, unstable scree in the sun, and the TRUE SUMMIT sits at its FAR RIGHT-HAND END, not at the high point directly above where you enter it. Finish on scree and snow. Negative markers: if you have roped up and are travelling on ice with crevasses, you are on the glacier variation on the northeast side of the peak; if you are still walking a grassy crest with no need to leave it, you have not reached the contour yet and are short of the basin.

bivy.name: Heart Lake
bivy.notes: The most useful camp in the whole zone for a climber. It sits just under eight miles in, a short climb below the High Divide, and it is the last camp on maintained trail with easy water before the route to Mount Carrie, Ruth Peak and Mount Fairchild leaves the trail for good. From here you gain the divide, follow it past Cat Peak, cross the exposed class 3 ridge known as the Catwalk, and the climbing starts. Parties who miss the permit sometimes take a Seven Lakes Basin camp such as Lunch Lake instead, but that puts you off the direct line and adds side-hilling in the morning. Fill every bottle here — the stretch from the divide out to the first Bailey Range camps carries no running water.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake and the creek feeding it, all season; this is the last dependable running water for a long way
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, QUOTA camp booked for a specific night on the federal booking site. Reservations for the summer season open in the spring and the High Divide camps are among the fastest to go in the park, often within minutes. Bear canisters mandatory, no campfires.
bivy.capacity: A small number of designated sites under a nightly cap, with a vault toilet; group parties must use the designated group site

bivy.name: Cat Basin
bivy.notes: Cat Basin lies just below the junction at roughly 5,042 ft where the High Divide trail meets the way into the Bailey Range, so it is the last sheltered ground on the approach before the route turns cross-country beneath Cat Peak. Parties heading for Mount Carrie use it to shorten the following morning and to get below the wind, since the divide itself is fully exposed. It is genuinely primitive — expect to be finding your own flat spot on durable ground, and expect the sites to be scattered rather than obvious. In heavy snow years the basin fills late and the traverse out to the Catwalk holds steep snow well into July.
bivy.water: Streams in the basin early in the season, unreliable by late summer; carry from Heart Lake if the year has been dry
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required. This one is worth phoning the park's wilderness information office about rather than assuming — the primitive and cross-country parts of this area are not all bookable through the standard online map, and staff issue those permits directly. Bear canisters mandatory, campfires banned outright at this height.
bivy.capacity: A primitive designated area rather than a developed camp; a handful of tent spots, no toilet you should count on

bivy.name: Sol Duc Hot Springs Resort campground
bivy.notes: The drive-in staging base for every objective in this zone except Mount Angeles, a couple of miles short of the end of the Sol Duc Hot Springs Road where the trailhead for the High Divide and Appleton Pass sits. Climbers use it the night before, because the walk to Heart Lake or Appleton Pass is long enough that leaving Port Angeles in the morning wastes the day. It opens with the season, roughly late March into late October, and it fills solidly on summer weekends. It is a staging base and nothing more — from here you still have the entire approach ahead of you, and every camp above it is permit-controlled.
bivy.water: Potable water and flush toilets in the comfort stations through the operating season
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit — this is a frontcountry campground with a nightly fee, taken on the federal recreation booking site or through the resort. Park entrance fee applies. Fires are allowed in the provided rings here, unlike anywhere you are going above it.
bivy.capacity: Around 82 tent sites plus a smaller RV loop; most tent sites are reservable and a handful are held back first-come

bivy.name: Boston Charlie's Camp
bivy.notes: This is the first camp on the far side of the Catwalk and the recognised start of the Bailey Range proper. It matters because it puts you directly at the foot of Mount Carrie's southwest ridge, where the route gains around 2,000 ft in under a mile on a semi-cairned bootpack, so a party camped here can be on the summit early and off the loose ground before the afternoon. Getting to it means crossing the exposed class 3 ridge between Cat Peak and Carrie with a full pack, which is the crux of the approach for most people and not somewhere to be in wet weather. The water is the honest drawback and the reason some parties push straight through to the basins beyond.
bivy.water: Poor and the standing complaint about the place — a shallow sinkhole pond that is often silty and stagnant, and nothing else nearby. Filter and treat, and consider carrying from Heart Lake or Cat Basin
bivy.permit: Covered by an Olympic wilderness cross-country permit, which for the Bailey Range is arranged directly with the park's wilderness information office rather than booked as a named campsite online. Bear canisters mandatory. No fires. Camp on durable surfaces — snow, rock or gravel — and pack out everything.
bivy.capacity: Informal cross-country bivy sites for a couple of small parties; no facilities of any kind

backups.name: Northeast Slopes / Goat Rocks crest
gear: microspikes or light crampons (recommended into at least mid-July for snow/moat crossings near the col)
hazards: exposure on the crest
afternoon thunderstorms
loose, chossy volcanic andesite on the south face
lingering snowfields and a glacier moat crossing near the Old Snowy-Ives col into July
off-trail routefinding with no maintained summit trail
backups.overview: Ives Peak (7,920+ ft) is the fourth-highest summit in the Goat Rocks Wilderness, sitting on the main crest between Old Snowy Mountain (7,880+ ft) to the north and Gilbert Peak (Mt. Curtis Gilbert), 8,184 ft, the range high point to the south. The peak straddles the Lewis/Yakima county line and is an eroded remnant of the Goat Rocks volcanic complex, an extinct stratovolcano active from roughly 3.2 million to 500,000 years ago; glaciation and hydrothermal alteration have since stripped away most of its outer flanks, exposing resistant volcanic dikes and spines. A small remnant glacier, the McCall Glacier, clings to Ives' northeast slope and feeds the Tieton River, while the west-facing slopes drain to the Cispus River. There is no maintained trail to the summit and nothing technical is required, but Ives sees only a fraction of the traffic of neighboring Old Snowy Mountain because of the off-trail travel and routefinding involved.
backups.beta: The easiest way up Ives Peak is a scramble. The standard approach follows the Pacific Crest Trail / Goat Rocks crest, which runs close to the peak's western slopes, then leaves the crest at the col northwest of the peak and follows the northwest ridge and a short south-face scramble to the summit; this is unroped class 2-3 talus/scree, not a technical rock or ice route. The ridge north of the summit is rocky and wind-scoured, with a short loose section near the col, and snow lingers on the peak's flanks into early summer.
backups.turnaround: As with any exposed alpine ridge scramble, set a turnaround time that gets you off the crest and below treeline before typical afternoon thunderstorm build-up, and before deteriorating visibility on featureless talus terrain.
backups.face: Northwest ridge and upper south face of Ives Peak, reached from the Old Snowy-Ives col on the Goat Rocks crest
backups.permit: Free self-issue Goat Rocks Wilderness permit at trailheads and ranger stations; Northwest Forest Pass or day fee at several trailheads.
backups.descent: Downclimb the Class 3 south face and Class 1-2 northwest ridge back to the Old Snowy-Ives col, then either reclimb Old Snowy's south ridge to close the loop over its summit, or contour around Old Snowy's west flank on scree to rejoin the PCT; return south on the PCT and Snowgrass Trail to the trailhead.
obj_haz: loose rock/talus ('choss') near the ridge col
lingering snow into early summer on north/east aspects
afternoon thunderstorm exposure typical of open Cascades ridgelines

waypoints.note: Bridge crossing of Goat Creek on the Snowgrass Trail in forest cover; a reliable water source about 2 miles in.

waypoints.name: Lower Snowgrass Flat / Lily Basin Trail (#86) junction
waypoints.note: The lower edge of Snowgrass Flat, which is closed to camping; a spring at the head of Snowgrass Creek (about a quarter mile off-trail) is the last dependable water before the ridge.

waypoints.name: Pacific Crest Trail junction
waypoints.note: Snowgrass Trail meets the PCT; head north toward Old Snowy Mountain to reach the Ives approach ridge.

waypoints.name: Old Snowy - Ives col
waypoints.note: Saddle between Old Snowy Mountain and Ives Peak where the north ridge route onto Ives begins; also the top of the Class 1-2 northwest ridge used on the descent.

waypoints.name: Southwest face ramp traverse
waypoints.note: Drop off the ridge crest onto a loose ramp and traverse roughly 40 ft climber's right below the summit cliff; exposed Class 3 terrain, loose underfoot.

waypoints.name: Ives Peak summit
waypoints.note: Broad rocky true summit (7,920+ ft) with views of Mt. Adams, Mt. Rainier, and the McCall Glacier on the northeast face.

sectionBreakdown.note: Alpine start with a light pack up to the PCT and Old Snowy's north ridge, stash poles for the final Class 3 scramble to the summit, downclimb the south ridge to the Old Snowy-Ives …

backups.detailed_rack: No technical rack is used on the standard route; it is an unroped, non-technical scramble.
pro_tips: Most parties combine Ives with Old Snowy Mountain in one day via the connecting col rather than climbing Ives in isolation
Start pre-dawn — the Old Snowy-Ives crest is fully exposed, a bad place to be caught in a Cascades afternoon thunderstorm
Carry an ice axe and microspikes through at least mid-July for the moat/snowfield crossing near the col
watch_out: Chossy, loose andesite on the Class 3 south face — test holds before weighting them
Exposed ledge/gap traverse below the summit notch
No bail-out shelter on the open crest if thunderstorms build
McCall Glacier moat/snow bridge near the Old Snowy-Ives col can be tricky in early-mid summer
backups.pro_needs: None — the standard route has no fixed protection or belays; consider an ice axe if snow still lingers on the crest or the peak's north/east-facing terrain early in the season.
backups.best_season: Late July through September for reliable snow-free travel; snowfields on the approach and the glacier moat near the Old Snowy-Ives col can persist into July in heavy-snow years, and the range averages roughly 25-40 ft of snow most winters.
backups.approach: Start at the Snowgrass Trailhead (aka "Berry Patch," elev. ~4,600 ft), reached via FR-21 (Johnson Creek Road) off US-12 about 3 miles west of Packwood. From the trailhead, follow the Snowgrass Trail #96 south then east through dense forest; the trail drops slightly (~75 ft) to cross Goat Creek on a footbridge/plank crossing around the 2-mile mark (only real water crossing on the approach, and a reliable water source — top off here or at the creeks in upper Snowgrass Flat). Continue climbing through subalpine forest and meadow to Lower Snowgrass Flat, then Upper Snowgrass Flat at roughly 6,400 ft (about 4 miles / ~1,800 ft gain from the trailhead) — a broad, popular wildflower meadow, closed to camping, with multiple small creeks (last dependable water before the ridge). From Upper Snowgrass Flat, continue about 0.3–0.5 mile further to the junction with the Pacific Crest Trail. Follow the PCT north to about 6,700 ft, then leave it and head off-trail to the northeast, ascending talus and scree with no defined tread (occasional cairns) toward the low col on the ridge crest between Old Snowy Mountain and Ives Peak — expect loose, unconsolidated talus that shifts underfoot; test holds and footing carefully. From the col, follow the ridge crest or a line just south of it (Class 2) over a rounded intermediate high point toward Ives' northwest ridge. At the base of the true summit block, a boot path threads up scree toward a notch between two rock outcrops; above the notch is a short cliff band — downclimb slightly and traverse a narrow, exposed ledge (Class 2) to gain the upper south face, then scramble roughly 40 ft to climber's right on loose blocky rock and up easy terrain to the 7,920-ft summit. Snowfields commonly linger on the approach slopes and in the col well into July (this basin can hold 25–40 ft of winter snowpack), so an ice axe is worth carrying for early/mid-season attempts on the traverse.
backups.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line: downclimb the loose Class 3 upper south face and the exposed ledge/cliff-band notch back to the northwest ridge, then follow the ridge crest back toward the Old Snowy–Ives col. From the col, most parties either (a) drop directly southwest through the scree/talus basin to regain the PCT — faster but the loosest, choss-iest line, or (b) traverse back over to Old Snowy Mountain and descend its established south-ridge boot path to the PCT near the Packwood Glacier bench, which several trip reports recommend specifically to avoid the worst loose rock directly below Ives' summit block. Either way, once back on the PCT, retrace it south to the Snowgrass Trail #96 junction and follow Snowgrass Trail #96 back down through Upper/Lower Snowgrass Flat and the Goat Creek crossing to the trailhead. This is entirely a scramble walk-off/downclimb — no fixed anchors, bolts, or rope work are involved or needed on this route. Primary descent hazards are the same loose talus/scree encountered on the ascent (higher consequence going downhill) and lingering snow/ice in the col and on the ridge crest into early-mid summer; a short glissade or scree-ski of the basin below the col is a common (optional) shortcut for the descent when snow-free.
backups.bail: Retreat is straightforward along the same ridge/crest used for the ascent back toward Old Snowy Mountain and the maintained trail system below; there are no fixed rappel anchors on this route since it is unroped scramble terrain.

itinerary.cal: Free self-issue wilderness permits at the trailhead; the upper Snowgrass basin is typically not fully snow-free until mid-to-late July, and Snowgrass Flat proper is closed to camping so camp at established sites in the upper basin or off-trail on durable ground.

days.note: From the Snowgrass Flat/Berry Patch trailhead (4,650 ft), cross Goat Creek at ~2 mi, pass (but don't camp at) Lower Snowgrass Flat around 4 mi, and continue climbing through meadows to the PCT, dropping a light camp in the upper Snowgrass basin around 7,100-7,200 ft. Afternoon is free to scout the next day's route to Elk Pass and enjoy the meadows and wildflowers.
days.title: Backpack in to upper Snowgrass basin camp
days.objective: Reach camp near treeline below the PCT/Elk Pass junction

days.note: Alpine start with a light pack up to the PCT and Old Snowy's north ridge, stash poles for the final Class 3 scramble to the summit, downclimb the south ridge to the Old Snowy-Ives col, then climb Ives' NW ridge (Class 1-2) and a short Class 3 south-face scramble to the top. Reverse the traverse back to camp, break camp, and hike the full ~6.5 mi back out to the trailhead.
days.title: Old Snowy + Ives Peak summit push, then hike out

schedule.label: Leave camp
schedule.detail: Light day pack, rejoin the PCT toward Elk Pass.

schedule.label: Stash poles, start Old Snowy scramble
schedule.detail: Unmarked junction; final ~50 ft is Class 3 hand-climbing.

schedule.label: Summit Ives Peak
schedule.detail: Via NW ridge (Class 1-2) and a short Class 3 south-face scramble.

schedule.label: Back at camp, break camp and hike out
schedule.detail: Arrive back at trailhead by ~4:30-5:00 PM.

days.objective: Tag both summits and hike all the way back to the trailhead

itinerary.totalNote: A 2-day trip: backpack ~7 mi into an upper Snowgrass basin camp (~7,100-7,200 ft) on Day 1, then do a long ~7-8 hr summit push over Old Snowy Mountain and Ives Peak and hike all the way out on Day 2 (~14.2 mi / 3,400 ft round trip total). Very fit parties do sometimes push it car-to-car in one long (8+ hr) day, but backpacking in is the standard/recommended plan.

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass ($5/day or $30/yr) or America the Beautiful interagency annual pass ($80) required to park at the Snowgrass Flat/Berry Patch trailhead; wilderness entry itself is free.
access.rules: Group size (people + stock combined) is capped at 12. Camping is prohibited within Snowgrass Flat itself and within 100 ft of the PCT or any lake shoreline (Dana Yelverton Shelter excepted). Campfires are banned in Shoe Lake Basin, at Dana Yelverton Shelter, and within 1/4 mile of Goat Lake.
access.permit: Free, self-issued wilderness permit at the trailhead kiosk (Snowgrass Flat/Berry Patch) — required for all Goat Rocks Wilderness entries, no quota.
access.closures: Forest Road 2150 (the spur to Chambers Lake/Berry Patch/Snowgrass Flat trailheads) is gated and closed to wheeled vehicles each winter for snow-recreation use, typically into early June depending on snowpack — check Gifford Pinchot NF road alerts before an early-season trip.
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful Interagency Pass

overnight_permit.what: Free self-issue Goat Rocks Wilderness permit
overnight_permit.where: Fill one out at the trailhead. Camping on Snowgrass Flat itself is prohibited; use the sites below it.

road.name: Forest Road 21 (Johnson Creek Rd) to Forest Road 2150
road.status: Open seasonally (gravel); FR 2150 gated in winter
road.driveNote: From US-12 about 2-3 miles west of Packwood (or ~17 mi east of Randle), turn onto FR 21 and follow gravel — washboarded in spots, notably the ~6 mi stretch from Cat Creek Campground to the FR 23 junction — roughly 13-15.5 miles to FR 2150; continue on FR 2150 to the Snowgrass Flat/Berry Patch loop trailhead near Chambers Lake, about 20 miles total from the highway.
road.seasonalGate: FR 2150 is closed to wheeled vehicles and reserved for winter snow recreation roughly November-early June (exact reopening depends on snowpack); confirm current status via Gifford Pinchot NF road alerts before an early-season attempt.

climate.typical: High alpine crest climate: cool mornings, intense UV, and a real risk of building afternoon cumulus/thunderstorms in summer, typical of the southern WA Cascades crest.

bySeason.fall: Can offer stable, snow-free conditions into September/early October, but shortens daylight and raises early-storm risk.
bySeason.spring: Wilderness typically still snowbound; the FR 2150 access road is gated for winter/spring use.
bySeason.summer: Prime window (Jul-Sep); usually snow-free on the route by mid-to-late July, with afternoon thunderstorm risk peaking Jul-Aug.
bySeason.winter: Inaccessible by normal means — FR 2150 gated and the crest holds deep snowpack (avg. ~25-40 ft seasonally).

emergency.notes: No cell service within the wilderness; the nearest reliable signal is along US-12 near Packwood or Randle. Fastest self-rescue is back down the Snowgrass Trail to FR 21/2150 and out to US-12.
emergency.county: Lewis (west/approach side); the summit sits on the Lewis-Yakima county line, with the McCall Glacier and east slopes in Yakima County.
emergency.rangerStation: Cowlitz Valley Ranger District, Gifford Pinchot National Forest — (360) 497-1103, 10024 US Hwy 12, Randle, WA (limited office hours: Mon/Wed/Fri).
emergency.nearestHospital: Arbor Health / Morton Hospital, Morton, WA — roughly 35-40 miles / about 1 hour drive from the Snowgrass Flat trailhead via US-12.
emergency.sheriffDispatch: 911 (Lewis County Sheriff's Office coordinates backcountry search and rescue for this side of the wilderness).

crowds.peakTraffic: Weekends July-August are busiest on the approach trails; the crest scramble to Ives sees noticeably less traffic than Old Snowy, and mid-week (Tue-Thu) is markedly quieter
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Old Snowy/Snowgrass Flats corridor sees heavy summer foot traffic (hundreds of hikers most weekends), but only a fraction continue the exposed scrambling onto Ives Peak itself — realistically dozens of parties per season complete the Old Snowy-Ives(-Gilbert) crest traverse

fitnessSpec.hiking: Long alpine day — typically 10-14+ miles with 4,000-5,000+ ft gain when combined with Old Snowy/Gilbert as part of the Goat Rocks crest traverse
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Light daypack, roughly 15-25 lbs (layers, extra food/water, helmet, possibly axe/microspikes early season)

partner_requirements.approachTime: Multi-hour approach via Snowgrass Flats or Goat Ridge/Berry Patch before reaching the Old Snowy/Ives crest; full traverse is typically a long single day or overnight trip
requiredSkills: Unroped Class 2-3 scrambling on loose, exposed rock
Comfort with sustained exposure along a narrow crest
Route-finding on an unmarked/braided ridge with cairns only intermittently
Helmet use for rockfall from parties above
Snow travel and basic self-arrest if lingering early-season snow is present on shaded slopes
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Intermediate scrambler with prior Class 3 experience on loose alpine rock and comfort with sustained, unroped ridge exposure

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July through mid-September, once the crest and shaded gullies have melted out and before fall storms move in

July.reason: Within the best-season window, but shaded NE slopes/gullies can still hold snow early in the month

June.reason: Deep lingering snow; the crest can still be in near-winter condition and route-finding is harder

August.reason: Peak of the best-season window; most consistently snow-free and stable conditions

October.reason: Outside the best-season window; early snow and storms can quickly turn this into full winter mountaineering

September.reason: Still within the best-season window; stable but a shorter weather window before fall storms

weather.typical: Highly exposed alpine crest weather that can change rapidly with little shelter along the ridge
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms are common during the July-August window

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Sustained exposure along the narrow Goat Rocks crest with unroped Class 3 moves over loose rock; a slip risks a long fall, and rockfall from parties above is a real concern, hence helmet use

avalanche.zone: NWAC South Cascades forecast zone (regional coverage; no zone specific to Ives Peak/Goat Rocks itself)

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: No crevassed glacier travel on the standard northwest ridge/crest scramble, but the McCall Glacier on the NE flank reaches up toward the Old Snowy-Ives col, and early in the season its moat or edge may have to be crossed or skirted on the traverse from Old Snowy; stay on rock where you can

gaps: No documented first-ascent history for Ives Peak
Roundtrip mileage/elevation-gain figures are sourced from the popular combined Old Snowy + Ives trip, not an Ives-only ascent
No 2026-season trip reports confirming current McCall Glacier/moat conditions

Difficulty breakdown (physical/technical/exposure/commitment/routefinding) is a computed starting estimate derived from grade, pitch count, and route data on file -- not a researched or crowd-sourced rating. Users can blend in their own read via the UI.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: Start at the Snowgrass Trailhead (aka "Berry Patch," elev. ~4,600 ft), reached via FR-21 (Johnson Creek Road) off US-12 about 3 miles west of Packwood.

backups.rope_note: Class 2-3 scramble on loose volcanic rock; short exposed ledge traverse (~40ft) below the summit cliff band. Helmet recommended for rockfall on notoriously loose Goat Rocks rock.
backups.corrections: Terrain-based inference from SummitPost/willhiteweb/oregonhikers descriptions; no explicit gear list.

approach_variants.name: Snowgrass Trail, the PCT junction and the Old Snowy to Ives col
approach_variants.notes: Start at the Snowgrass trailhead, also called Berry Patch, at about 4,600 ft, reached by forest road off the highway west of Packwood. Follow Snowgrass Trail #96 south then east through dense forest; it drops slightly to cross Goat Creek on a plank crossing around the 2-mile mark, which is the only real water crossing and a reliable source. Climb through subalpine forest and meadow to Lower and then Upper Snowgrass Flat at roughly 6,400 ft, about 4 miles in — a broad wildflower meadow, closed to camping, with small creeks, the last dependable water before the ridge. Continue a further 0.3 to 0.5 mile to the PCT junction, follow the PCT north to about 6,700 ft, then leave it and head off-trail northeast, ascending talus and scree with no defined tread and only occasional cairns, toward the low col on the crest between Old Snowy Mountain and Ives Peak. The talus is unconsolidated and shifts underfoot. Snowfields linger on the approach slopes and in the col well into July — this basin can hold 25 to 40 ft of winter snowpack — so an axe is worth carrying for early and mid-season attempts.
approach_variants.season: Roughly late Jul through mid-Sep, once the crest and shaded gullies have melted out
hazards: Loose, unconsolidated talus and scree with higher consequence on the descent
Chossy volcanic andesite on the summit south face
An exposed narrow ledge traverse below the summit, reached by downclimbing
Lingering snowfields and a moat crossing near the col into July
Off-trail route-finding with no maintained summit path
Exposure to afternoon thunderstorms on an open crest
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE COL BETWEEN OLD SNOWY AND IVES IS THE ARRIVAL, AND YOU GET TO IT BY LEAVING A TRAIL, NOT BY FOLLOWING ONE.

Leave the PCT north of the Snowgrass Trail junction, at roughly 6,700 ft, and go off-trail NORTHEAST up talus. There is no tread. Occasional cairns are the only marks. If you are still on maintained trail you have not started the route.

YOU KNOW YOU ARE AT THE COL BECAUSE YOU ARE BETWEEN TWO PEAKS at about 7,250 ft — Old Snowy behind you, Ives ahead. A high point on one side only is not the col.

THE BUMP IS THE TRAP AND IT IS COUNTABLE: from the col the ridge crosses a ROUNDED INTERMEDIATE HIGH POINT before you reach the true summit block. THAT BUMP IS NOT THE SUMMIT. If you have not passed one rounded bump, you have not reached the summit block, whatever the ground in front of you looks like.

THE BASE OF THE SCRAMBLE IS A NOTCH BETWEEN TWO ROCK OUTCROPS, reached by a boot path up scree. And here is the test that settles it beyond doubt, because it is the opposite of what you expect at a summit block: ABOVE THE NOTCH IS A SHORT CLIFF BAND, AND THE ROUTE GOES DOWN FIRST. You downclimb slightly and traverse a narrow, exposed ledge to gain the upper south face, then scramble about 40 ft to climber's right on loose blocky rock to easy ground and the summit.

SO: IF THE LINE IN FRONT OF YOU ONLY GOES UP, YOU ARE AT THE WRONG NOTCH. Having to lose a little height at the notch is the confirmation.

DESCENT FINDING WORTH MAKING BEFORE YOU START: dropping straight southwest off the col into the basin is faster and is the loosest ground on the mountain. Traversing back over Old Snowy and down its established south-ridge path avoids the worst of it.

climbing_route.label: Ridge crest from the col
climbing_route.notes: From the low col on the crest between Old Snowy Mountain and Ives Peak, follow the ridge crest or a line just south of it over a rounded intermediate high point toward Ives' northwest ridge. Snowfields commonly linger in the col well into July, so an ice axe is worth carrying for early/mid-season attempts on the traverse.

climbing_route.label: Notch and exposed ledge traverse
climbing_route.notes: At the base of the true summit block a boot path threads up scree toward a notch between two rock outcrops; above the notch is a short cliff band — downclimb slightly and traverse a narrow, exposed ledge to gain the upper south face.

climbing_route.label: Upper south face to summit
climbing_route.notes: Scramble roughly 40 ft to climber's right on loose blocky rock, then up easy terrain to the 7,920-ft summit.

bivy.name: Snowgrass Flat area backcountry camps
bivy.notes: The standard base for Old Snowy and Ives Peak, and for the West Route on Gilbert. The name misleads: the flat proper is a closed meadow and the legal camping is in the timber and on the benches a little below it, around 6,000 to 6,300 feet, roughly three to four miles from the road. From here Old Snowy is a walk-up on a spur off the crest, Ives is a scree-and-ridge scramble off the col between the two, and Gilbert is a long committing day traversing goat ledges across Cispus Basin at 7,400 to 7,600 feet before the southwest slope. This is the most heavily used corner of the wilderness and the parking fills on weekdays, so arriving Friday evening for a Saturday climb is a poor plan. The meadows hold snow into July in a normal year, which is pleasant for the scrambles and awkward for finding a dry pitch.
bivy.water: Goat Creek and its tributaries run through the basin and are reliable well into the season; treat everything
bivy.permit: Goat Rocks Wilderness permit, free and self-issued from the box at the trailhead — no reservation and no fee. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park at Berry Patch or the Snowgrass trailhead. CAMPING WITHIN SNOWGRASS FLAT ITSELF IS PROHIBITED, along with camping within 100 feet of the Pacific Crest Trail and within 100 feet of any lake. Camp only in pre-existing sites.
bivy.capacity: Numerous established sites in the timber and benches below and around the meadow; no quota and no numbered pads, so capacity is whatever the pre-existing sites hold, and on summer weekends that is fully subscribed

bivy.name: Chambers Lake Campground
bivy.notes: The obvious drive-in base for the Goat Rocks crest, under a mile from both the Berry Patch and Snowgrass trailheads, so you can sleep at the car and be walking at first light without the four-mile carry to Snowgrass. That makes it the right choice for a car-to-car attempt on Old Snowy, and a sensible staging night before shouldering a pack for Ives or Gilbert. It is heavily timbered and low, so there is no view and no acclimatisation value, and the approach roads are long gravel with washboard — allow more driving time than the mileage suggests. Snow closes the access road well into spring, which is the practical limit on early-season attempts from this side.
bivy.water: No potable water on site — bring your own or filter from the lake. Vault toilets are provided
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit needed for the campground itself, since it sits outside the boundary. A modest per-night fee has been charged in some seasons and waived in others, so carry cash and check the board on arrival. A Northwest Forest Pass is still required at Berry Patch and the Snowgrass trailhead a short distance up the road.
bivy.capacity: A small forested campground with basic single and double sites; first come, first served

bivy.name: Lower Snowgrass Flat / Lily Basin Trail (#86) junction

backups.name_search: northeast ne slopes goat rocks crest

backups.name: Southeast Slopes / Standard Scramble
hazards: Wet-slab and cornice avalanche danger in the gullies during spring snow season
Loose talus, scree, and some loose rock in the summit gullies
Seasonal waterfall/creek crossing at the base of the west gully descent line
Afternoon thunderstorms common on the exposed ridge in summer
No reliable cell coverage in the Rainy Pass/Washington Pass corridor
backups.overview: A non-technical summit on the Okanogan Range crest between Rainy Pass and Washington Pass, in Chelan County within the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest. Whistler is linked by a high ridge to Cutthroat Peak (8,050 ft), 0.8 mile north-northeast, and offers a broad, mostly-talus scramble popular as an early-season warm-up or a corn-snow ski descent in late spring. The standard route climbs the mountain's south ridge and southwest slope; a steeper alternative ascends a broad gully system visible from Rainy Pass.
backups.beta: From a roadside turnout on SR-20 (or alternatively the Rainy Pass PCT trailhead), a boot path climbs through open forest and a meadow basin, then rises on a traversing line to intersect the level part of Whistler's south ridge at about 6,180 ft. From there the route follows the ridge and adjoining gullies — staying north of a loose gully band and using a visible ramp near the headwall — to the 7,790 ft summit; an alternative continues the ridge to about 6,800 ft before cutting left across gullies onto gentler terrain on the southwest slope for the final push. It is class 3 scrambling throughout, with class 4 moves possible depending on line choice.
backups.turnaround: In spring/early summer when the gullies still hold snow, turn around by late morning to avoid wet-slab avalanche release as the sun softens the snowpack; on the dry-season south-ridge route, the main time pressure is afternoon thunderstorm buildup over the crest.
backups.permit: No climbing or wilderness permit required; Northwest Forest Pass (or day fee) to park at developed trailheads.
backups.descent: Reverse the ascent route down the south ridge / southwest slope.
obj_haz: Cornices along the upper ridge and gully rims in winter/spring
Wet, heavy maritime snow prone to wet-slab avalanches

waypoints.name: Meadow rising traverse
waypoints.note: Boot path climbs through an open meadow then angles into a rising traverse aiming for the crest of Whistler's south ridge; faint tread, easy to lose in fog.

waypoints.name: South ridge gain point
waypoints.note: Boot path tops out on the level section of Whistler's south ridge here; from this point the route follows the ridge and connecting gullies toward the summit.

waypoints.name: 6,800 ft ridge/gully split
waypoints.note: Ridge steepens; here parties can cut left across gullies onto the gentler southwest slope as an easier alternative to staying directly on the ridge crest.

waypoints.name: Summit ridge scramble band
waypoints.note: Class 2-3 terrain mixes downsloping slabs and loose gravel on ledges just below the summit ridge; a helmet is worth carrying for rockfall and slip potential here.

waypoints.name: Rainy Pass Trailhead (PCT North parking lot, SR-20)

sectionBreakdown.note: A single-day round trip from the SR-20 turnout east of Rainy Pass (about 5,000 ft): climb through a meadow to gain the south ridge around 6,180 ft, then follow rock and gully terra…

backups.detailed_rack: No roped protection is used on the standard scramble route; parties typically carry trekking poles for the meadow/traverse sections, a helmet for the loose ridge and gully terrain, and an ice axe (with willingness to turn back if conditions warrant crampons) when snow lingers in the gullies in early season.
what_to_bring: Ice axe and traction (crampons/microspikes) for snow-covered gullies in spring/early summer
Layers for an exposed, wind-prone ridge
pro_tips: The Rainy Pass PCT-lot gully approach doubles as a well-regarded spring corn-snow ski descent — go early enough to catch the snow softening but before it turns to mush
On the south-ridge route, cutting left across gullies at ~6,800 ft onto the southwest slope avoids the harder gully scrambling higher on the ridge crest
watch_out: Trailhead access disappears entirely once SR 20's winter gates close (roughly late Nov–late Apr/mid-May) — check WSDOT pass status first
The unmarked highway pullout for the south-ridge route is easy to miss; it's 3.1 miles east of Rainy Pass and 0.7 mile before the Blue Lake trailhead
Early-season (May-June) ascents will find the gullies holding consolidated snow — carry an ice axe and know how to self-arrest
The west-gully descent funnels toward a seasonal waterfall — exit right into the glades to avoid it
backups.pro_needs: None — this is an unroped Class 3 scramble with no fixed protection or technical rack; a rope and basic protection could be carried by conservative parties for the class 4 variations, but are not standard.
backups.approach: Two trailheads serve the Southeast Slopes / South Ridge scramble, both off SR-20 between Rainy Pass and Washington Pass. Option A (PCT approach, most commonly used): park at the marked Pacific Crest Trail North trailhead lot on the north side of Rainy Pass (~4,850 ft, next to the Road 600 turnoff). From the lot, leave the PCT almost immediately and strike out cross-country/climber's-path east into open forest, gaining steeply through timber and over downed logs — there is no maintained tread once you leave the PCT. Continue up through the trees (expect lingering snow patches into early summer) to about 6,100 ft, where the forest opens into a meadow basin below the west ridge/gully complex. From the basin, trend south/southeast on a rising traverse to gain the col/basin between Whistler and the southwest peak of Cutthroat, then work up the broad west ridge or the shallow gully just north of it to the summit shoulder; the final short section involves a rock gully with a visible ramp along the headwall over downsloping slabs and loose gravel — a helmet is recommended here for rockfall from parties above. Round trip via this line runs roughly 3.7 miles with about 3,000 ft of gain (trailhead 4,850 ft to summit 7,790 ft). Option B (highway turnout approach, reaches the true south ridge): from the unmarked pullout on SR-20 about 3.1 miles east of Rainy Pass (0.7 mile before the Blue Lake trailhead, ~5,000 ft), walk back down/along the road shoulder to a boot path that starts at the west edge of a stand of trees. Follow the boot path up through a meadow, then rising-traverse to intersect the level portion of Whistler's south ridge at about 6,180 ft. From there, scramble up the ridge and connecting gullies to the summit; alternatively leave the ridge around 6,800 ft, cross a couple of gullies left (west) onto gentler southwest-facing slopes, and finish to the summit that way. This line is also about 4 miles round trip with ~3,000 ft gain. Both approaches are trail-less above the first stretch of forest — expect route-finding, loose talus/scree in the gullies, and class 2-3 terrain with occasional class 3-4 moves and real exposure near the ridge crest and summit gully; no reliable water source above the lower forest, so carry what you need from the car. No creek fords or avalanche paths of note on the standard summer line, but early-season snow lingers in the forest and basin and can make the gully sections firm or icy.
backups.descent_text: There is no rappelling on the standard Southeast Slopes/South Ridge route — it's a walk-off/downclimb, reversing whichever line was used on the way up. From the summit, downclimb the summit gully (loose gravel and downsloping slabs — take care with rockfall for anyone below) back to the shoulder, then descend either the west ridge/gully back into the meadow basin and forest (Option A) or drop onto the south ridge and retrace the rising traverse back to the meadow and boot path to the highway turnout (Option B). Loose rock and talus in the gullies is the main descent hazard — down-climb facing in on the steeper class 3 sections and stay alert for parties below. Some ski mountaineers descend a separate snow-filled west gully (~35°, over 1,000 ft of sustained fall-line terrain funneling to a waterfall lower down, requiring an exit right into the glades to avoid the falls) as a spring ski descent, but that is a snow-season variant, not part of the standard summer scramble descent, and should not be used as a hiking descent once snow is out. rappels: 0.
backups.bail: Retreat is straightforward by reversing the scramble at any point; no committing technical sections.

pitch_detail.notes: Boot path from the SR-20 turnout, leaving from the west edge of a stand of trees and climbing up through a meadow.
Rising traverse across the meadow/talus to intersect the level part of the south ridge at 6,180 ft.

Follow the ridge and adjoining gullies to the 7,790 ft summit, staying north of the loosest gully band and using a visible ramp to bypass rock near the headwall; an alternative cuts left at ~6,800 ft onto gentler southwest-slope terrain.

itinerary.cal: Snow often lingers in the summit gullies into early-mid summer; best conditions are typically July-September once SR-20 (Rainy Pass) has been open a while and gullies have melted out.

days.note: A single-day round trip from the SR-20 turnout east of Rainy Pass (about 5,000 ft): climb through a meadow to gain the south ridge around 6,180 ft, then follow rock and gully terrain (class 3-4) to the 7,790 ft summit before reversing the same line back to the car. No camping is involved — this is done entirely car-to-car.
days.title: Car-to-car scramble

schedule.label: Leave the SR-20 turnout
schedule.detail: Park at the unmarked pullout on SR-20 about 3.1 miles east of Rainy Pass (~5,000 ft), walk back along the shoulder and pick up the boot path at the west edge of a stand of trees.

schedule.detail: Rising traverse through meadow to intersect the level part of the south ridge near 6,180 ft.

schedule.label: Class 3-4 gully/ridge scrambling begins
schedule.detail: Follow the ridge and connecting gullies, staying on rock where possible; snow may linger in gullies into early summer.

schedule.label: Summit (7,790 ft)
schedule.detail: Views of Cutthroat Peak, Liberty Bell, and the Washington Pass area; typical lunch/break stop.

schedule.label: Begin descent
schedule.detail: Reverse the ascent line down the south ridge.

schedule.label: Back at trailhead
schedule.detail: Total car-to-car time roughly 6-8 hours depending on snow conditions and pace.

days.objective: Summit Whistler Mountain via the South Ridge and return to the highway turnout

itinerary.totalNote: A moderate single-day scramble: about 4 miles round trip with 3,000 ft of gain, typically 6-8 hours car-to-car from the highway turnout; no overnight component.

access.fees: $5/vehicle/day at the Rainy Pass trailhead (cash/check or digital day pass); Northwest Forest Pass and Interagency (America the Beautiful) passes also honored.
access.notes: Not inside North Cascades National Park — this corridor is entirely Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District). No Mount Rainier-style climbing fee applies here.
access.rules: No climbing or wilderness permit required for day climbing. Dispersed camping capped at 10 days; no camping within ¼ mile of Cutthroat Lake; no campfires at dispersed sites; bear-resistant food storage required; dogs on leash ≤6 ft.
access.permit: No permit required for day scrambling.
access.closures: Entire approach is inaccessible whenever SR 20 is under its winter closure (roughly late Nov through late Apr/mid-May); confirm current road status with WSDOT before driving in.
access.seasonal: WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) closes gate-to-gate roughly early December–mid/late April; the entire Washington Pass corridor is car-inaccessible in winter.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Methow Valley Ranger District (Winthrop, WA)
access.land_manager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Washington Pass Overlook, Blue Lake, and Cutthroat trailheads — $5/day or $30/annual (America the Beautiful pass also honored).
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass or $5 day-use fee at Rainy Pass trailhead

overnight_permit.where: A Northwest Forest Pass, an America the Beautiful pass, or a Recreation.gov day pass covers parking at the Rainy Pass PCT North trailhead; no permit paperwork is needed to camp anywhere along this stretch of the Pacific Crest Trail.

road.name: North Cascades Highway (SR 20)
road.status: Paved highway, open only when seasonal snow gates are up
road.driveNote: Drive SR 20 over Rainy Pass; the two trailhead options (Rainy Pass PCT lot, or the unmarked pullout 3.1 mi east of the pass) are both directly off the highway with no additional dirt-road driving.
road.seasonalGate: Gated closed for winter — gates at Diablo (west) and Early Winters near Mazama (east). Typically closes late November and reopens late April to mid-May depending on snowpack; check WSDOT's pass report before planning a trip.

climate.fall: Cools quickly with possible early-season snow at elevation; SR-20 access can end abruptly with the season's first significant highway closure.
climate.spring: Snowpack still substantial into May/June on north- and gully-facing terrain; the west-facing gully is a documented corn-snow ski descent in late May.
climate.summer: Generally dry with occasional afternoon thunderstorms typical of the eastern Cascades crest; the standard scramble window.
climate.winter: SR-20 gated/closed through the Washington Pass-Rainy Pass corridor; the peak is inaccessible by the standard trailhead.
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate with a strong maritime influence even on this east-slope Cascades peak; winter and spring snow tends to be wet and heavy, producing high avalanche danger on the gullied approaches. Summers are typically dry with mostly clear skies, though afternoon thunderstorms can build over the Cascade crest.

bySeason.fall: Good scrambling into September/early October; watch for early-season snow and shortening daylight.
bySeason.spring: Deep, often unstable wet snow fills the gullies (used for ski descents); avalanche and cornice hazard is significant — check NWAC before going.
bySeason.summer: Typical dry-scramble season once snow clears the upper slopes, usually by mid-to-late July; talus and scree underfoot.

emergency.notes: Cell coverage is unreliable to absent in the Rainy Pass/Washington Pass corridor; the nearest reliable help is the highway itself — flag down traffic or drive to Mazama/Winthrop. This stretch of SR 20 is remote and, once winter gates close, entirely inaccessible.
emergency.county: Chelan County (summit); the SR 20 approach corridor runs along the Chelan/Okanogan county line near Rainy and Washington Passes
emergency.rangerStation: Methow Valley Ranger District, 24 West Chewuch Rd, Winthrop, WA, (509) 996-4000
emergency.nearestHospital: Three Rivers Hospital, 507 Hospital Way, Brewster, WA — 24-hour ER, (509) 689-2517
emergency.sheriffDispatch: Okanogan County Sheriff (trailhead/highway side) — for backcountry incidents, contact via 911; confirm jurisdiction may hand off to Chelan County SAR depending on exact location

crowds.peakTraffic: weekends July-September; the Rainy Pass PCT trailhead itself sees heavy thru-hiker and day-hiker traffic, but most of that traffic splits off and does not continue up toward Whistler's summit gully
crowds.estimatePerSeason: roughly 20-50 parties per season (estimate) - a known but secondary North Cascades scramble objective, well behind trade routes like Mailbox Peak or Colchuck

fitnessSpec.hiking: Able to sustain ~4 miles round trip with ~3,000 ft of gain at elevation (trailhead near 4,850 ft, summit 7,790 ft), typically a 6-9 hour round trip
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Light day pack (10-20 lb) - water, layers, helmet; no technical rack needed in normal summer conditions

partner_requirements.approachTime: 2-3 hours from the Rainy Pass PCT trailhead to the base of the summit gully, then additional time for the talus scramble to the top
requiredSkills: basic navigation off-trail once leaving the PCT
self-arrest/step-kicking awareness for lingering early-season snow patches
afternoon-thunderstorm judgment (turnaround discipline on an exposed summit)
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Comfortable, unroped Class 3 scrambler; should have prior experience on loose talus/scree and basic alpine routefinding, since the route is a gully/slope scramble rather than a maintained trail to the top

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through early October, once snow has melted off the upper slopes

July.reason: Snow typically clears from the upper gully by mid-July; long daylight and stable summer weather, though early-July ascents can still hit lingering snowfields

August.reason: Most reliable month - talus fully exposed, driest conditions, though afternoon thunderstorms are common and should be watched for

October.reason: Early season snow can return to the high pass terrain at any time, days are short, and North Cascades Highway/access conditions become less predictable

September.reason: Still generally dry and clear with fewer bugs and crowds than midsummer, but shorter daylight and first frosts begin

weather.typical: Typical North Cascades crest weather at ~7,800 ft: cool mornings, warm midday, and rapid weather swings; the Washington Pass area is prone to sudden cloud buildup even on otherwise clear forecasts
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms are common in July-August - plan for an early start and to be off the summit before storms build

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Low-to-moderate: Class 2-3 scrambling terrain, but the loose talus and scree footing creates real twisted-ankle and rockfall-onto-partner risk, especially in the gully where parties stack above one another; lingering early-summer snowfields can add a slip hazard on the approach gully before full melt-out

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer scramble route; NWAC does not issue forecasts for this zone/period since the route is climbed outside the Nov-May avalanche season

gaps: No confirmed first-ascent date or party found
Exact county boundary (Chelan vs. Okanogan) at the summit itself not independently confirmed beyond Wikipedia
No public GPS track found for this route as of this research pass.

Difficulty breakdown (physical/technical/exposure/commitment/routefinding) is a computed starting estimate derived from grade, pitch count, and route data on file -- not a researched or crowd-sourced rating. Users can blend in their own read via the UI.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the PCT North trailhead parking at Rainy Pass on SR-20 (~4,860 ft)

backups.rope_note: Non-technical: boot path from SR-20 near Rainy Pass up through meadows to the south ridge (6180ft), then ridge/gully scrambling to the summit. No roped climbing required.

approach_variants.name: Rainy Pass PCT lot, then cross-country east into the meadow basin and the col toward Cutthroat's southwest peak
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the marked Pacific Crest Trail North trailhead lot on the north side of Rainy Pass at about 4,850 ft, next to the Road 600 turnoff. LEAVE THE PCT ALMOST IMMEDIATELY and strike out cross-country east into open forest, gaining steeply through timber and over downed logs. There is no maintained tread once you leave the PCT.

This is WHISTLER MOUNTAIN ABOVE RAINY PASS in Chelan County, not the Whistler Canyon trailhead area near Oroville, which is about 100 miles away and unrelated.

Round trip runs roughly 3.7 miles with about 3,000 ft of gain.
hazards: No maintained tread above the PCT; route-finding the whole way
Downed logs in the lower forest
Loose talus and scree in the gullies, with class 3-4 moves and real exposure near the ridge crest
Downsloping slabs and loose gravel in the summit gully
No reliable water above the lower forest
Early-season snow lingering in the forest and basin, firming the gullies
approach_variants.baseFinding:
CLIMB UNTIL THE FOREST OPENS. At about 6,100 ft the timber gives way to A MEADOW BASIN BELOW THE WEST RIDGE AND GULLY COMPLEX, and that transition is the first reliable confirmation on a trail-less approach. Trees stopping is something you notice in any visibility.

FROM THE BASIN, TREND SOUTH AND SOUTHEAST ON A RISING TRAVERSE TO GAIN THE COL AND BASIN BETWEEN WHISTLER AND THE SOUTHWEST PEAK OF CUTTHROAT. THAT COL IS THE AIMING POINT, and it is named by the two peaks either side of it.

Then work up the BROAD WEST RIDGE, or the SHALLOW GULLY JUST NORTH OF IT, to the summit shoulder.

THE LAST SECTION IS THE ONE THAT CONFIRMS YOU ARE ON THE SUMMIT LINE RATHER THAN A NEIGHBOURING GULLY: A ROCK GULLY WITH A VISIBLE RAMP ALONG THE HEADWALL, OVER DOWNSLOPING SLABS AND LOOSE GRAVEL. A ramp cutting the headwall is the way through; helmet on here for rockfall from parties above.

approach_variants.name: The unmarked SR-20 turnout, then a boot path onto the true south ridge at 6,180 ft
approach_variants.notes:
The second option, and the one that reaches the true south ridge. From the unmarked pullout on SR-20 about 3.1 miles east of Rainy Pass, 0.7 mile BEFORE the Blue Lake trailhead, at about 5,000 ft, walk back down and along the road shoulder to a boot path that starts at the WEST EDGE OF A STAND OF TREES.

About 4 miles round trip with roughly 3,000 ft of gain, the same as the PCT option.
hazards: An unmarked trailhead identified only by its distance from the Blue Lake trailhead
Trail-less above the first stretch of forest
Class 2-3 with occasional class 3-4 moves and real exposure near the ridge crest
Loose talus and scree in the connecting gullies
No reliable water on the route
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TRAILHEAD IS UNMARKED AND THE PATH START IS A TREE-LINE EDGE, SO THE FIND IS AT THE ROAD RATHER THAN ON THE MOUNTAIN. The pullout is 0.7 MILE BEFORE THE BLUE LAKE TRAILHEAD coming from Rainy Pass. IF YOU HAVE REACHED THE BLUE LAKE TRAILHEAD, YOU HAVE DRIVEN 0.7 MILE TOO FAR. From the pullout, walk the shoulder to where a STAND OF TREES begins, and the boot path leaves from its WEST EDGE.

FOLLOW THE BOOT PATH UP THROUGH A MEADOW, THEN RISING-TRAVERSE TO INTERSECT THE LEVEL PORTION OF WHISTLER'S SOUTH RIDGE AT ABOUT 6,180 FT. A LEVEL SECTION OF RIDGE IS THE ARRIVAL, and a level stretch on a ridge is something you can feel underfoot without seeing anything.

FROM THERE, SCRAMBLE UP THE RIDGE AND CONNECTING GULLIES TO THE SUMMIT. THE ALTERNATIVE, WHICH IS ALSO CORRECT: leave the ridge around 6,800 ft, cross a couple of gullies LEFT, west, onto gentler southwest-facing slopes, and finish that way.

SO THE DECISION AT 6,800 FT IS A REAL FORK AND BOTH BRANCHES WORK: stay on the crest for more exposure and directness, or cross two gullies west for easier ground.

THE NEGATIVE TEST AGAINST THE OTHER APPROACH, WHICH MATTERS BECAUSE BOTH START WITHIN THREE MILES OF EACH OTHER ON THE SAME HIGHWAY: the PCT option leaves from the marked PCT North lot at Rainy Pass and gains a MEADOW BASIN at 6,100 ft below the WEST ridge. This one leaves from an unmarked turnout and gains the SOUTH ridge at 6,180 ft. Marked lot and west ridge, or unmarked turnout and south ridge.

climbing_route.label: Col to the summit shoulder via the west ridge (Option A)
climbing_route.notes: From the meadow basin at about 6,100 ft trend south/southeast on a rising traverse to gain the col/basin between Whistler and the southwest peak of Cutthroat, then work up the broad west ridge or the shallow gully just north of it to the summit shoulder. Trail-less with route-finding and loose talus/scree in the gullies, and real exposure near the ridge crest; early-season snow can make the gully sections firm or icy.

climbing_route.label: Final rock gully and headwall ramp
climbing_route.notes: The final short section involves a rock gully with a visible ramp along the headwall over downsloping slabs and loose gravel — a helmet is recommended here for rockfall from parties above.

climbing_route.label: South ridge from 6,180 ft (Option B)
climbing_route.notes: Intersect the level portion of Whistler's south ridge at about 6,180 ft, then scramble up the ridge and connecting gullies to the summit; loose talus/scree in the gullies and real exposure near the ridge crest and summit gully.

climbing_route.label: Southwest slopes variant
climbing_route.notes: Alternatively leave the ridge around 6,800 ft, cross a couple of gullies left (west) onto gentler southwest-facing slopes, and finish to the summit that way.

bivy.name: Rainy Pass PCT north trailhead
bivy.notes: Everything starts from this lot. It is also the start of Whistler Mountain, which is unlike the rest: head east from the parking area into the second gully and follow it to the summit, about four miles round trip and three thousand feet of gain, and no camp helps in the slightest. There is a toilet and no water. Parties routinely sleep in the car here before a long PCT day. As with everything on this stretch of SR 20, access is governed by the winter closure — the highway shuts in late November or early December and normally reopens between mid April and early May, though a bad winter can push it very much later, so confirm before driving. Note also that this specific trailhead has been closed at times for roadwork in recent seasons, which strands the entire zone when it happens.
bivy.water: None at the lot, and this matters more here than it looks. The crest north of the pass is dry, so what you carry out of the car is what you have until well down the far side.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. No camping permit, no quota and nothing to reserve anywhere in this zone — this is national forest, and the park permit system that governs the country west of here does not apply.
bivy.capacity: A large paved lot on the north-east side of the highway at the pass, shared between climbers, larch-season day hikers and long-distance walkers. It fills early on weekends from late summer onward and there is no overflow.
